advances: For constant geometric midpoint penalty on a parity matching, the full original cubic atom sum loses at most an exponential in the squared penalty parameter, while the geometric-mean-row weighted variance is at most an absolute constant times the penalty parameter times its squared logarithm plus one. Both estimates are uniform over all positive weights satisfying the midpoint identities, including arbitrary affine spatial tilts of the convex spike-penalty blocks. This supplies the two linked estimates in the assigned bridge without a product composition or an unrestricted convex-support depth assertion.

proof:
Let \(\mathcal J\) be the set of midpoints of the distinct same-parity pairs. Every endpoint belongs to at most one such pair, since its parity class has at most two points. The endpoint sets of the pairs are therefore pairwise disjoint. The midpoint hypothesis makes each \(j\in\mathcal J\) the center of exactly one pair, whose endpoints we denote by \(u_j,v_j\).

If \(x\ne j\) and \(x,2j-x\in\mathcal A\), those two points are distinct and have the same parity. Their midpoint is \(j\). Distinctness of pair midpoints therefore shows that \(R_j=\lbrace u_j,j,v_j\rbrace\) when \(j\in\mathcal J\), and \(R_j=\lbrace j\rbrace\) otherwise. This verifies the matching-row hypotheses of accepted fact 4d36c889dd0a9ba2 with exactly the aliases in the statement. An atom can be both a center and an endpoint, but that does not create an additional pair with the same center.

The zero displacement in (2) gives \(H_p(j)\ge p_j>0\). Consequently \(b(p)\ge\sum_{x\in\mathcal A}p_x^3>0\), and every quantity in (2) is well-defined. Reflection \(x\mapsto2j-x\) preserves \(\kappa_j\) and reverses \(Y_j\), proving \(\mathbb E_{\kappa_j}Y_j=0\).

First prove atom retention. Write \(a_3=\sum_{x\in\mathcal A}p_x^3\). For \(\alpha\in B_m\), let \(r_\alpha=\sum_{x\in\mathcal A\cap(\alpha+2\mathbb Z^m)}p_x\), allowing \(r_\alpha=0\), and put \(\mathcal Q=\sum_{\alpha\in B_m}r_\alpha^3\). Since there are exactly \(K\) parity classes and their masses sum to one, Jensen's inequality gives \(\mathcal Q\ge K^{-2}\).

Every non-singleton parity class is one pair \(\lbrace u_j,v_j\rbrace\), so expansion of its mass cubed and (1) give the exact identity
$$
\mathcal Q
=a_3+3\sum_{j\in\mathcal J}p_{u_j}p_{v_j}(p_{u_j}+p_{v_j})
=a_3+3t^2\sum_{j\in\mathcal J}p_j^2(p_{u_j}+p_{v_j}).
\tag{6}
$$
For nonnegative \(a,r\), the inequality \(3a^2r\le2a^3+r^3\) follows from \(2a^3+r^3-3a^2r=(r-a)^2(r+2a)\ge0\). Apply it in (6) with \(a=p_j\) and \(r=p_{u_j}+p_{v_j}\). The centers are distinct, and the pair masses belong to distinct parity classes. It follows that
$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathcal Q
&\le a_3+t^2\left(
2\sum_{j\in\mathcal J}p_j^3
+\sum_{j\in\mathcal J}(p_{u_j}+p_{v_j})^3\right)\\
&\le(1+2t^2)a_3+t^2\mathcal Q.
\end{aligned}
\tag{7}
$$
The two estimates in the second line are separate. Thus a center that is also an endpoint causes no overcounting error.

Put \(\delta=t^2\). For \(0<\delta\le1/2\), rearranging (7) and using \(\mathcal Q\ge K^{-2}\) gives
$$
K^2a_3\ge\frac{1-\delta}{1+2\delta}\ge e^{-4\delta}.
\tag{8}
$$
For the last inequality, \(1+2\delta\le e^{2\delta}\), and \(1-\delta\ge e^{-2\delta}\) on \([0,1/2]\): the function \(\log(1-\delta)+2\delta\) vanishes at zero and has derivative \((1-2\delta)/(1-\delta)\ge0\) there.

For \(1/2\le\delta\le1\), the parity cardinality assumption gives \(|\mathcal A|\le2K\). Jensen's inequality applied to the original atom probabilities yields \(a_3\ge|\mathcal A|^{-2}\), hence \(K^2a_3\ge1/4\). Also \(e^2\ge1+2+2=5>4\), so \(1/4\ge e^{-2}\ge e^{-4\delta}\). This proves the first inequality of (3) for the entire interval, including its endpoints. If the pair family is empty, (6) simply reads \(\mathcal Q=a_3\), and the same proof remains valid.

Next prove the sparse row price. For \(j\in\mathcal J\), put \(z_j=\frac12\log(p_{v_j}/p_{u_j})\). Equation (1) gives
$$
p_{u_j}=t p_je^{-z_j},\qquad
p_{v_j}=t p_je^{z_j},\qquad
p_{u_j}^3+p_{v_j}^3=2t^3p_j^3\cosh(3z_j).
\tag{9}
$$
The kernel masses at \(u_j,j,v_j\) are respectively \(t/(1+2t),1/(1+2t),t/(1+2t)\), and the scores are \(-z_j,0,z_j\). Thus the exact identities are
$$
H_p(j)=(1+2t)p_j,\qquad
V_j=\frac{2t z_j^2}{1+2t},\qquad
p_jH_p(j)^2V_j=2t(1+2t)p_j^3z_j^2.
\tag{10}
$$
At every singleton row the score and its variance are zero.

Let \(\rho=\log(1/t)\ge0\). We claim that every real \(z\) satisfies
$$
z^2\le2\rho^2+4t^3\cosh(3z).
\tag{11}
$$
If \(|z|\le\rho\), this follows from \(z^2\le\rho^2\). Otherwise put \(a=|z|-\rho>0\). The exponential series gives \(e^{3a}\ge(3a)^2/2\ge a^2\), while
\(t^3\cosh(3z)=e^{-3\rho}\cosh(3|z|)\ge e^{3a}/2\). Therefore
$$
z^2=(\rho+a)^2
\le2\rho^2+2a^2
\le2\rho^2+2e^{3a}
\le2\rho^2+4t^3\cosh(3z),
$$
proving (11), also when \(t=1\) and \(\rho=0\).

Combine (9)--(11), sum over the nontrivial rows, and use the zero variances on all other rows. The numerator of the exact auxiliary average in (2) satisfies
$$
\begin{aligned}
\sum_{j\in\mathcal A}p_jH_p(j)^2V_j
&=2t(1+2t)\sum_{j\in\mathcal J}p_j^3z_j^2\\
&\le4t(1+2t)\left(
\rho^2\sum_{j\in\mathcal J}p_j^3
+\sum_{j\in\mathcal J}(p_{u_j}^3+p_{v_j}^3)\right)\\
&\le4t(1+2t)(1+\rho^2)a_3\\
&\le12t(1+\rho^2)b(p).
\end{aligned}
\tag{12}
$$
The second inequality uses the distinct centers and the disjoint endpoint sets separately. A point that serves in both roles is charged at most \(\rho^2\) times its cube in the first sum and once in the second, exactly as allowed by the factor \(1+\rho^2\). The final inequality uses \(t\le1\) and \(a_3\le b(p)\). Dividing by the original \(b(p)>0\) proves the second inequality of (3). Empty pair families give zero on the left of (12), without an exception or a change of probability law.

Finally verify (5). Accepted fact 4d36c889dd0a9ba2 proves for exactly the block objects (4) that every parity class of \(T_m\) has at most two points, and that all its distinct same-parity pairs are
\(\lbrace c,c+2e_{i_m(c)}\rbrace\) for \(c\in C_m^{\mathrm{bool}}\cap D_m\). Their midpoints \(F_m(c)\) are supported Boolean points and are distinct by injectivity of \(F_m\). Thus these full complete block supports satisfy every geometric hypothesis above.

For the weights in (5), the endpoint \(c\) and the midpoint \(j=F_m(c)\) are Boolean, while \(c+2e_{i_m(c)}\) is a spike. With the single block normalizer \(Z\) in (5), their original probabilities obey
$$
\sqrt{p_c p_{c+2e_{i_m(c)}}}
=\frac{\sqrt{\epsilon_i}\,
e^{\gamma\cdot(c+e_{i_m(c)})}}{Z}
=\sqrt{\epsilon_i}\,p_{F_m(c)}.
\tag{13}
$$
Thus (1) holds with \(t=\sqrt{\epsilon_i}\) for every spatial field. Every atom of \(T_m\), including singleton parities and centers that also serve as endpoints, retains the probability in (5). Applying the proved estimates with \(\mathcal A=T_m\) proves the asserted block application.
statement:
Let \(m\ge1\) be an integer, put \(K=2^m\), and let \(\mathcal A\subset\mathbb Z^m\) be finite and nonempty. Assume every class modulo \(2\mathbb Z^m\) contains at most two points of \(\mathcal A\). For every unordered pair \(\lbrace u,v\rbrace\) of distinct same-parity points of \(\mathcal A\), assume its midpoint \(j=(u+v)/2\) belongs to \(\mathcal A\), and assume different such pairs have different midpoints. Centers are allowed to be endpoints of other pairs. The pair family is allowed to be empty. These hypotheses apply in particular to complete convex lattice supports with the stated parity and midpoint properties.

Choose weights \(w_x>0\) for every \(x\in\mathcal A\), and define the original probability law by \(Z=\sum_{x\in\mathcal A}w_x\), \(p_x=w_x/Z\) on \(\mathcal A\), and \(p_x=0\) off \(\mathcal A\). Suppose one number \(0<t\le1\) satisfies
$$
\sqrt{p_up_v}=t p_j
\qquad\left(j=\frac{u+v}{2}\right)
\tag{1}
$$
for every distinct same-parity pair. Equivalently, \(\sqrt{w_uw_v}=t w_j\) for every such pair, with exactly the same \(t\).

Use the one-block definitions of accepted fact 4d36c889dd0a9ba2, with the explicit aliases \(L=1\), \(n_1=m\), \(A_1=\mathcal A\), \(w_{1,x}=w_x\), \(Z_1=Z\), and \(p_1=p\). Thus, for every \(j\in\mathcal A\), define
$$
\begin{aligned}
R_j&=\lbrace x\in\mathcal A:2j-x\in\mathcal A\rbrace,\\
H_p(j)&=\sum_{v\in\mathbb Z^m}\sqrt{p_{j+v}p_{j-v}}
       =\sum_{x\in R_j}\sqrt{p_xp_{2j-x}},\\
b(p)&=\sum_{j\in\mathcal A}p_jH_p(j)^2,\\
\kappa_j(x)&=\frac{\sqrt{p_xp_{2j-x}}}{H_p(j)}\quad(x\in R_j),\\
Y_j(x)&=\frac12\log\frac{p_x}{p_{2j-x}},\qquad
V_j=\mathbb E_{\kappa_j}Y_j^2,\qquad
q_j=\frac{p_jH_p(j)^2}{b(p)}.
\end{aligned}
\tag{2}
$$
The reflected sum is oriented: opposite nonzero displacements both occur and zero occurs once. The score has mean zero, so \(V_j\) is its variance. The law \(q\) and the row laws \(\kappa_j\) are auxiliary and retain precisely the normalization in (2).

Then the full original atom sum and the row price satisfy
$$
K^2\sum_{x\in\mathcal A}p_x^3\ge e^{-4t^2},
\qquad
\sum_{j\in\mathcal A}q_jV_j
\le12t\left(1+\log^2\frac1t\right).
\tag{3}
$$
In particular the two requested bounds hold with the common absolute constant \(C=12\).

For the block application, retain exactly \(B_m,D_m,F_m,i_m,E_m,T_m,C_m^{\mathrm{bool}}\) of accepted fact 4d36c889dd0a9ba2, for any chosen symmetric saturated chain partition, including the prescribed standard partition. Thus
$$
\begin{aligned}
B_m&=\lbrace0,1\rbrace^m,\qquad
F_m(c)=c+e_{i_m(c)},\qquad c_{i_m(c)}=0,\\
E_m&=\lbrace c+2e_{i_m(c)}:c\in D_m\rbrace,\\
T_m&=\operatorname{conv}(E_m)\cap\mathbb Z^m
     =E_m\mathbin{\dot\cup}C_m^{\mathrm{bool}},\qquad
C_m^{\mathrm{bool}}=\operatorname{conv}(E_m)\cap B_m.
\end{aligned}
\tag{4}
$$
For every \(\gamma\in\mathbb R^m\) and every spike penalty \(0<\epsilon_i\le1\), the entire block law
$$
p_x=\frac{e^{\gamma\cdot x}\epsilon_i^{\mathbf1_{\lbrace x\in E_m\rbrace}}}{Z},
\qquad
Z=\sum_{x\in C_m^{\mathrm{bool}}}e^{\gamma\cdot x}
  +\epsilon_i\sum_{x\in E_m}e^{\gamma\cdot x}
\qquad(x\in T_m)
\tag{5}
$$
satisfies (3) with \(\mathcal A=T_m\) and \(t=\sqrt{\epsilon_i}\). Here \(\epsilon_i\) denotes the spike penalty, not a height deviation, and \(Z\) is only this block normalizer; it does not replace any original serial normalizer \(W\).
